newsitem.title: MEXICO: Boss of N.Y. deaf exploitation ring is deaf -report.
newsitem.headline: Boss of N.Y. deaf exploitation ring is deaf -report.

text.p: A Mexican wanted for leading a smuggling ring believed to have forced Mexican deaf mutes into servitude in New York is himself deaf, family members of one of his alleged victims said on Monday.

Pilar Santiago, sister of 22-year-old deaf mute Ismael Santiago Garcia, told Mexico's Radio Red her brother was persuaded to go to work in the United States by an apparently trustworthy man she identified as Mr. Paoletti.

"(Paoletti) is a very good person, or at least that is how he appeared when I went to see him. He's a very noble man, and as he is deaf -- well, one never would have thought he would do such a thing," she said in a live interview.

Police in the United States and Mexico were searching for Reinaldo Paoletti, believed to be the leader of an operation that recruited deaf mutes from homes and schools in Mexico and smuggled them into the United States. The smuggling ring was uncovered after U.S. officials found 57 people in two cramped apartments in the New York borough of Queens on Saturday.

Authorities said there were indications they had been persuaded to come to the United States on the promise of a better life, but instead were forced under threat of beatings to work as vendors of trinkets like key chains, baseballs, pens and toys in New York City's streets and subways.
They were allowed to keep only 20 percent of the takings, while those running the operation kept the remainder.
It was not clear whether the Paoletti referred to by Santiago was Reinaldo, but she described the man she dealt with as someone in his 50s or early 60s.
Of seven people arrested in the case, four were members of the Paoletti family.
Santiago said Paoletti informed her brother he would be working in a bazaar in the United States. "He never specified what kind of bazaar."
Her brother Ismael, she said, met Paoletti and considered him a friend. "From one day to the next, (Ismael) made up his mind to leave," she said. "He didn't even warn us."

Santiago's mother, identified only as Mrs. Garcia, told Radio Red that Ismael had been taken to Los Angeles from Mexico on May 9, 1996, and that she only received a photograph of him three months after he arrived.
"I was always deeply worried because I would go to (Paoletti's) house and they always told me he wasn't there, and that they didn't know where he was," she said.

The mother said she was still unsure whether her son was among those found in the Queens apartments. Of the 57 rescued, 27 were men, 18 were women and 12 were children ranging in age from six months to 16 years, officials said.
